Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: Five years ago, at sixty-three, Rangi had been driving home from a late audit on a stretch of interstate when a tanker jackknifed ahead of him. The impact was instantaneous and violent to the body. He woke to the thick, acrid stench of ruptured diesel and burning rubber, darkness pressing against the cracked windshield, and the distant, rhythmic whine of a twisted exhaust pipe echoing through the trapped cabin. He spent hours prying at his door until help broke through, but the cold dread of being trapped had already seared itself into his nervous system, ensuring that the specific sensory markers of that night would remain permanently potent. In the months that followed, the sensory landscape of his old life became a minefield. The mere scent of diesel fumes from a passing transit bus, the sudden plunge of an elevator into a shadowed shaft, or even the low rumble of a semi-truck merging onto the highway would instantly drag the accident out of the past and into the present. The memory did not visit him as a recollection; it hijacked his awareness, forcing him to feel the heat and hear the shattering glass as though he were still pinned in the metal cabin. As these sensory ambushes compounded, Rangi had come to believe he could not survive another collapse of control, convincing himself he had to be on guard all the time and that he must be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. His attempt to protect himself directly altered his internal landscape. He was certain that if he thought about the event, he would not be able to handle it, so he forced his mind away from the wreck the moment it flickered. But that deliberate suppression fractured his focus, leaving him mentally exhausted and paradoxically more likely to be triggered without warning. The pressure of maintaining this vigilance quickly bled into his physical state. Rangi found that his unyielding need to stay alert kept his nervous system perpetually wound, which in turn caused his body to react to danger before he had even had time to think. His pulse would spike, his muscles would lock, and a cold sweat would break across his back before his conscious mind could even register what he was sensing. This physiological alarm state quickly became the engine of his daily existence. The constant physical readiness wore him down, lowering his threshold for distress and making the intrusive memories feel even more immediate and unavoidable. When the memories did break through, they arrived with such visceral intensity that they recalibrated his attention, making him hypersensitive to the low hum of ventilation systems, the shadow of a closed office door, and the distant sound of idling delivery trucks. His habit of scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building, combined with his body reacting before he could think, kept his attention fixed on the periphery, ensuring he never missed a sudden shift in traffic or a lingering chemical odor. At his corner desk, cross-referencing portfolio risk models, he spent his hours staring at the double doors and fire exit signs rather than the financial ledgers, his avoidance of the overpass growing into a rigid routine of alternate routing. By the time he finally sat in my office, Rangi had stopped driving past the highway junction, had begun flinching at the sound of his wife’s car pulling into the driveway, and had grown distant from his family. He came because the fatigue had become unbearable and because the sheer effort of staying alert was costing him his focus at work and his peace at home. What frightened him most was the terror that if he ever let his guard down even for a moment, the darkness, the smell, and the noise would return, and he would once again be trapped with no way out. He hoped, however, that someone could help him untangle the loop he had spent years building, so he could finally stop bracing for the crash and simply live.
